title: Hybrid VPC Peering and Split-Tunnel Reference Architecture for Private Deployments
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview:

This document describes a reference architecture and operational playbook for hybrid private deployments of Redwood Inference that combine direct VPC peering with split-tunnel egress for telemetry and control-plane traffic. The goal is a reproducible pattern that preserves customer network isolation, minimizes cross-VPC egress cost, and provides predictable operational controls for day‑2 operations.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: Private control-plane + data-plane topologies for medium to large customers (10–500 GPUs).
- Audience: Solutions engineering, private deployment SRE, networking, security, and customers' networking teams.

Design goals:
- Ensure tenant traffic (inference requests & KV cache traffic) remains private within customer VPCs or dedicated peered networks.
- Allow controlled outbound connections for telemetry, control-plane, and staged package updates using split-tunnel proxies.
- Provide explicit failure modes and fallback behaviors for transient peering/route issues.
- Keep observable, auditable routing decisions with standardized metric names and alert thresholds.

Architecture summary (text diagram):

  Customer VPC A (Private Subnet CIDR 10.10.0.0/16)          Redwood Managed Peering VPC (10.20.0.0/16)
  +-------------------+                                       +-------------------------------+
  | Inference Pods    | <--- VPC peering (bi-directional) --> | Dedicated inference pools     |
  | (k8s nodes)       |                                       | (dedicated GPUs)              |
  +-------------------+            
         |
         |---> Split-tunnel proxy (Envoy) --(TLS mTLS)--> Telemetry egress (Redwood telemetry collectors)

Notes: Peering is limited to tenant CIDRs and managed peering VPC ranges. Split-tunnel proxy owns per-subnet routing for outbound-only flows (telemetry/control-plane) and marks metrics with egress_tag.

Key components and responsibilities:
- Customer VPC routers: enforce CIDR and security group restrictions. Provide static routes to Redwood peered ranges.
- Peering fabric (Redwood): BGP-enabled peering or AWS VPC peering depending on cloud region. Maintains routing ACLs and advertised prefixes per-customer.
- Split-tunnel proxy: lightweight Envoy sidecar or node-level proxy that:
  - routes inference traffic to local k8s services or peered Redwood pools,
  - routes telemetry/control-plane to Redwood collectors via TLS+MTLS,
  - enforces egress allowlist (IP ranges and ports).
- Identity & auth: Mutual TLS for egress; IAM role-based registration for VMs/k8s nodes; KMS integration for customer-encrypted keys.
- Observability: local and remote metrics, traces, and structured audit logs. See Observability section below.

Routing and peering modes (decision matrix):
1) Full peering (default for Dedicated customers):
   - Use AWS VPC peering or cloud-equivalent, full route exchange for tenant CIDRs and Redwood serving subnets.
   - Advantages: low latency, no NAT.
   - Risks: broader blast radius if misconfigured. Restrict via route tables and security groups.
2) Partial peering + split-tunnel (recommended for regulated customers):
   - Peer only the serving subnets; all egress (telemetry/updates) uses split-tunnel proxies that route over outbound TLS to Redwood collectors.
   - Advantages: tighter control over peered prefixes; egress is explicit and auditable.
3) Overlay tunneling (fallback):
   - When direct peering is unavailable, fall back to mTLS-over-HTTPS tunneling for control plane.
   - Advantages: works across restrictive network setups; higher latency and cost.

Configuration table (example):
| Config key | Example value | Notes |
|------------|---------------|-------|
| tenant_cidr | 10.10.0.0/16 | Customer primary subnet used for inference nodes |
| peering_ranges | 10.20.0.0/24,10.20.1.0/24 | Redwood advertised ranges for serving pools |
| split_proxy_image | redwood/egress-proxy:v1.7.2 | Node-level proxy image; pinned in private deployments |
| egress_allowed_ports | 443, 853 | TLS (443) and DNS-over-TLS (853) for telemetry |
| mTLS_cert_role | redwood:private-deploy | Role used to request mTLS certs from internal CA |

Firewall and ACL guidance:
- Minimum open ports on inference subnets:
  - Inbound from peered ranges: TCP 443 (inference API), TCP 10250 (kubelet) only from management ranges.
  - Egress from split-tunnel proxy: TCP 443 to Redwood collectors; UDP 53 or TCP 853 for DNS (depending on operator preference).
- Deny all other inbound traffic by default.

Operational SLOs and telemetry:
- Network-level SLOs (for private deployments):
  - Peering connectivity: 99.95% monthly availability (measured as BGP adjacency up + route installed).
  - Egress tunnel availability (split-tunnel): 99.9% monthly for active nodes.
  - Token-latency (p95 end-to-end): < 120 ms for local inference when peering healthy. Documented fallbacks when above thresholds are violated.

Required metrics (standardized names):
- redwood.private.peering.adjacency_status (gauge: 0/1)
- redwood.private.splitproxy.egress_success_count (counter)
- redwood.private.splitproxy.egress_failure_count (counter)
- redwood.private.kvcache.hit_rate (gauge: percent)
- redwood.private.inference.latency_ms.p95 (histogram)

Alerting thresholds (examples):
- peering adjacency down for >2 minutes -> P1 alert to private-deploy-sre.
- splitproxy egress_failure_rate > 0.5% sustained for 5m -> P2 alert.
- kvcache.hit_rate drop > 10% relative to baseline for 15m -> P2.

Rollout and validation checklist (pre-deploy -> post-install):
1) Pre-deploy (Network + Security reviews)
   - Confirm customer CIDRs and approved peering_ranges.
   - Exchange and verify public keys for BGP (if using BGP).
   - Validate firewall rules with customer network team.
2) Deploy peering + route entries (automation):
   - Apply peering with limited CIDRs.
   - Configure split-proxy as a DaemonSet (k8s) or systemd service for VMs.
3) Validation tests (automated):
   - Route test: traceroute to serving pool IPs from a sample node. Expect <=3 hops for peered mode.
   - Egress test: curl --resolve to telemetry endpoint via split-proxy and verify TLS mutual auth succeeds.
   - Latency smoke: run perf harness generating 1000 short requests and measure p50/p95.
4) Canary and expansion
   - Start with 5% of nodes in peered route; monitor metrics for 24–72 hours.
   - Gradually expand to 100% with rolling restart preserving KV cache affinity.

Failure modes and mitigation:
- BGP flap or peering teardown:
  - Detection: redwood.private.peering.adjacency_status -> 0.
  - Mitigation: automatic update of route table to direct inference egress through overlay tunnel; scale up split-proxy instances to handle transient increase in egress.
- Split-proxy certificate expiry
  - Detection: mTLS handshake failures and increased egress_failure_count.
  - Mitigation: automated cert refresh job with 48‑hour renew window; emergency manual rotation steps documented below.

Emergency manual rotation steps (condensed):
1) SSH to control node with privileged key and run: 
   - /opt/redwood/pxctl cert rotate --role redwood:private-deploy --force
2) Confirm new cert via: curl -v --cert /etc/redwood/certs/node.crt https://collector.redwood.internal/healthz
3) If rotation fails, enable overlay tunneling and notify customer with expected degraded latency.

Observability and dashboards:
- Dashboards to create by default for private deployments:
  - Peering overview: adjacency_status, route counts, error events.
  - Split-proxy health: CPU/memory, egress_success/failure, handshake latencies.
  - Inference end-to-end: per-model p50/p95/p99 latency, token consumption, kvcache hit rate.
- Logs: Structured JSON including fields: node_id, tenant_id, egress_tag, request_id, route_path.
- Traces: parent spans for proxy->collector->serving-pool with explicit attributes: net.path, net.latency_ms.

Security and compliance notes:
- All egress traffic must be encrypted with mTLS; server certs pinned to Redwood CA.
- KMS-backed key wrap for private keys; HSM integration for FIPS customers available as opt-in.
- Audit logs exported to long-term retention for restricted customers as part of compliance packaging.

Testing and automation templates (examples):
- Example split-proxy DaemonSet snippet (k8s YAML, trimmed):
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: DaemonSet
  metadata:
    name: redwood-split-proxy
  spec:
    template:
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: envoy
          image: redwood/egress-proxy:v1.7.2
          env:
            - name: REDWOOD_COLLECTOR
              value: "collector-01.redwood.internal:443"

- Route verification playbook (ansible): ping, traceroute, and TLS handshake checks against known endpoints.

Ownership and contacts:
- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments team (oncall: private-deploy-sre).
- Escalation: eng-sre -> networks -> security.
- Runbook location: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/private-peering-runbook

Open decisions (for follow-up ADRs):
- Standardize whether BGP will be offered as GA or remain opt-in (tracking: ADR-2026-bgp-service-class).
- Define a default certificate rotation window (proposal: 30 days) and automate via control-plane.

Appendix A — Example commands and verification snippets:
- Check peering routes (AWS CLI example):
  aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters "Name=route.destination-cidr-block,Values=10.20.0.0/16"
- TLS handshake test with client cert:
  openssl s_client -connect collector-01.redwood.internal:443 -cert node.crt -key node.key -CAfile redwood-ca.pem

Appendix B — Allowed ports and protocols (quick reference):
| Destination | Source | Ports | Protocol | Purpose |
|------------|--------|-------|----------|---------|
| collector-01.redwood.internal | split-proxy | 443 | TCP/TLS | telemetry, control-plane |
| dns.redwood.internal | split-proxy | 853 | TCP | DNS over TLS |
| peered-serving-pool | inference-node | 443 | TCP | inference API |

Appendix C — Change log:
- 2025-11-12: Document created (Maya Chen).
- 2026-02-05: Added explicit SLOs and emergency rotation steps; tightened egress port guidance (reviewers: Diego Alvarez, Priya Nair).
